prompt: When NH3 donates its lone pair to BH3, the product H3N→BH3 is drawn with an arrow for the new bond. What does the arrow mean?

choices.text: It is bookkeeping that shows the electrons came from the base; the coordinate covalent bond is really an ordinary covalent bond
It shows the bond is ionic rather than covalent
choices.why: A coordinate covalent (dative) bond is a covalent bond. The arrow only records where the electrons came from.

choices.text: It shows that electrons move from BH3 to NH3
choices.why: The arrow points from the base to the acid, the direction of electron donation: from NH3 to BH3.

choices.text: It shows the bond is much weaker than a normal covalent bond
choices.why: The arrow says nothing about strength. A coordinate covalent bond is just an ordinary covalent bond like any other.

explanation: When a Lewis acid and base combine, the larger unit is an adduct and the new bond is a coordinate covalent or dative bond. It is often drawn with an arrow showing electron donation from base to acid. The arrow is a convenient formalism, a bookkeeping tool; the bond is an ordinary covalent bond.

prompt: How does the Lewis concept describe a Brønsted acid-base reaction such as the protonation of NH3?

choices.text: H^+ acts as a Lewis acid that accepts an electron pair from the base, forming an adduct
H^+ acts as a Lewis base that donates an electron pair to NH3
choices.why: H^+ has no electrons to donate. It accepts the lone pair of NH3, so it is the Lewis acid.

choices.text: It can't describe it, because no electron pair is involved
choices.why: The base's lone pair forms the new bond to H^+, so Brønsted reactions fit within the Lewis concept.

choices.text: NH3 acts as a Lewis acid, because it gains H^+
choices.why: NH3 donates its lone pair, so it is the Lewis base. H^+ is the electron-pair acceptor.

explanation: In Brønsted acid-base reactions the hydrogen ion is an acid because it accepts an electron pair from the Brønsted base. Under the Lewis concept, Brønsted reactions involve forming an adduct between H^+ and a base. Since H^+ usually starts out bound to another base, many are displacement reactions.

prompt: How does the Lewis concept describe the autoionization of thionyl chloride, 2SOCl2 ⇌ SOCl^+ + SOCl3^−?

choices.text: As a displacement reaction: a Cl^− base is transferred from one SOCl2 (leaving the Lewis acid SOCl^+) to another SOCl2 acting as a Lewis acid
As H^+ transfer from one SOCl2 to another
choices.why: SOCl2 contains no hydrogen. The group transferred is Cl^−, a lone-pair-bearing base.

choices.text: As electron transfer from one SOCl2 to another, a redox reaction
choices.why: No oxidation states change. A Cl^− with its electron pair moves between two Lewis acids.

choices.text: As formation of an adduct between SOCl^+ and SOCl3^−
choices.why: That adduct formation is the reverse reaction. Autoionization breaks an S–Cl bond and moves Cl^− to a second SOCl2.

explanation: In the autoionization of SOCl2, the S–Cl bond breaks to give a lone-pair-bearing Cl^− base and an SOCl^+ Lewis acid fragment. A second SOCl2 acts as a Lewis acid toward the liberated Cl^−, giving SOCl3^−. The Cl^− base is transferred between two Lewis acids, a Lewis acid-base displacement reaction.

prompt: In water, Al(OH)3 + OH^− → Al(OH)4^−. Which description of Al(OH)3 in this reaction is correct?

choices.text: It is a Lewis acid (at its Al^3+ center) and an Arrhenius acid, but not a Brønsted acid
It is a Brønsted acid, because it gives H^+ to OH^−
choices.why: No H^+ is transferred. OH^− bonds to the Al center, so Al(OH)3 acts as a Lewis acid, not a Brønsted acid.

choices.text: It is a Lewis base, because it has lone pairs on its hydroxide ligands
choices.why: Those lone pairs make Al(OH)3 a Lewis base toward H^+. In this reaction it accepts an electron pair from OH^− at Al.

choices.text: It is an Arrhenius base, because the product contains more hydroxide
choices.why: OH^− is removed from solution, which lowers [OH^−] and raises [H^+]. That makes Al(OH)3 an Arrhenius acid here.

explanation: Al(OH)3 forms an adduct with OH^− at its Al^3+ center, so it acts as a Lewis acid. No H^+ transfer occurs, so it is not acting as a Brønsted acid or base, but it is an Arrhenius acid because OH^− is consumed from solution. With H^+, Al(OH)3 instead acts as a Lewis base through its hydroxide lone pairs: it is amphoteric at different atomic centers.

prompt: How do the terms nucleophile and electrophile differ from Lewis base and Lewis acid?

choices.text: They describe Lewis bases and acids that react quickly with a given partner, so they are kinetic terms
They describe thermodynamic strength, the position of an acid-base equilibrium
choices.why: Thermodynamic propensity is what acid and base strength describe. Nucleophilicity and electrophilicity are about how fast a substance reacts.

choices.text: They apply only to inorganic reactions
choices.why: They are mostly used for organic reactions, though they also describe inorganic ones, such as hydroxide attacking chlorine.

choices.text: A nucleophile is a Lewis acid and an electrophile is a Lewis base
choices.why: It's the reverse: nucleophiles are Lewis bases and electrophiles are Lewis acids.

explanation: Thermodynamics determines which outcomes are possible; kinetics determines which happen quickly. Synthetic chemists call Lewis acids that react rapidly with a given Lewis base good electrophiles, and Lewis bases that react rapidly with a given Lewis acid good nucleophiles. This is sometimes called the Ingold-Robinson acid-base concept.

prompt: Toward electrophilic carbon in organic solvents, I^− is a good nucleophile. How does it rank as a Brønsted base among the halides?

choices.text: It is the weakest Brønsted base of the halides, since it is the conjugate base of the strong acid HI
It is the strongest Brønsted base, since good nucleophiles are always strong bases
choices.why: Nucleophilicity and basicity don't always track each other. For the halides the two orders are opposite.

choices.text: It is about as basic as F^−
choices.why: F^− is the strongest Brønsted base of the halides and I^− the weakest, even though I^− is the better nucleophile.

choices.text: It is not a Lewis base at all
choices.why: I^− donates an electron pair when it attacks carbon, so it is a Lewis base. It is simply a poor Brønsted base.

explanation: Acid-base strength and nucleophilicity are not the same thing. For the halides, the order of Brønsted basicity (F^− > Cl^− > Br^− > I^−) is the opposite of the order of nucleophilicity toward electrophilic carbon (I^− > Br^− > Cl^− > F^−). I^− is a good nucleophile but a poor Brønsted base, being the conjugate of the strong acid HI.

prompt: Under the Usanovich concept, how is Zn classified in 2[Fe(CN)6]^3− + Zn → 2[Fe(CN)6]^4− + Zn^2+?

choices.text: As a base, because Usanovich bases include reductants (electron donors)
As an acid, because it ends up as a cation
choices.why: Usanovich acids include oxidants (electron acceptors). Zn gives up electrons, so it is a base.

choices.text: It can't be classified, because no electron pair is donated
choices.why: The Usanovich concept removes the requirement that electrons be donated in pairs, so redox reactions count as acid-base reactions.

choices.text: As a Lewis base, because it donates a lone pair to [Fe(CN)6]^3−
choices.why: No adduct forms. Zn transfers electrons, which makes it a Usanovich base but not a Lewis base.

explanation: The Usanovich concept expands the Lewis definition by dropping the requirement that the electrons be a pair. Usanovich acids are Lewis acids plus oxidants, and Usanovich bases are Lewis bases plus reductants. Zn reduces [Fe(CN)6]^3− to [Fe(CN)6]^4−, so it is a base. Most chemists still find it more convenient to treat Lewis acid-base and redox reactions separately.

prompt: In the frontier orbital picture of H3N→BH3 adduct formation, what is the net result of the orbital interaction?

choices.text: Electrons from the NH3 HOMO (its lone pair) are stabilized in a new, lower-energy σ bonding MO formed with the BH3 LUMO
Electrons from the BH3 HOMO are donated into the NH3 LUMO
choices.why: BH3 is the acceptor. The donation runs from the base's HOMO (the NH3 lone pair) into the acid's LUMO.

choices.text: The NH3 lone pair is raised in energy into an antibonding MO
choices.why: The occupied orbital formed is a bonding MO, lower in energy, so the base lone pair is stabilized.

choices.text: No new MO forms; the lone pair stays localized on N
choices.why: Mixing the NH3 HOMO with the BH3 LUMO forms a bonding orbital between N and B.

explanation: The frontier orbital approach treats Lewis acid-base interaction as donation from the base's HOMO into the acid's LUMO. For NH3 and BH3, ammonia's a1 HOMO mixes with BH3's a2'' LUMO to form a lower-energy bonding orbital. Since it holds the electrons, the net result is lowering of the base's lone pair energy.

prompt: In the SN2 reaction of hydroxide with CH3Cl, how does the frontier orbital approach explain loss of the chloride leaving group?

choices.text: Electrons from the hydroxide HOMO populate the C–Cl antibonding LUMO of CH3Cl, breaking the C–Cl bond
Electrons from the CH3Cl HOMO move to hydroxide, breaking the C–Cl bond
choices.why: Hydroxide is the base (nucleophile) and donates electrons. CH3Cl's LUMO is the acceptor.

choices.text: Hydroxide removes H^+ from CH3Cl, which forces out Cl^−
choices.why: No H^+ transfer occurs in SN2 substitution. Hydroxide attacks carbon as a Lewis base.

choices.text: The C–Cl bonding orbital is filled further, making the bond stronger
choices.why: Adding electrons to an antibonding orbital weakens the bond. The CH3Cl LUMO is C–Cl antibonding.

explanation: From a frontier orbital perspective, the SN2 reaction between hydroxide and CH3Cl is a Lewis acid-base interaction. Donation of electrons from the hydroxide HOMO populates the antibonding CH3Cl LUMO, breaking the C–Cl bond and displacing the chloride leaving group.

prompt: Viewed with the frontier orbital approach, which reactant in a normal Diels-Alder reaction acts as the Lewis base?

choices.text: The diene, whose HOMO donates into the dienophile's LUMO
The dienophile, whose HOMO donates into the diene's LUMO
choices.why: Roles are reversed here. In a normal Diels-Alder reaction the diene is the donor (Lewis base) and the dienophile the acceptor (Lewis acid).

choices.text: Neither, because pericyclic reactions aren't acid-base reactions
choices.why: The frontier orbital approach shows that pericyclic reactions are Lewis acid-base reactions.

choices.text: The product cyclohexene
choices.why: Acids and bases are reactants. The diene is the Lewis base.

explanation: With the frontier orbital approach it becomes apparent that pericyclic reactions are Lewis acid-base reactions. In the Diels-Alder reaction the diene acts as a Lewis base and the dienophile as a Lewis acid, with the diene's HOMO donating into the dienophile's LUMO.

prompt: In the bonding between a metal with occupied d orbitals and a π-acceptor ligand such as CO, which roles do the metal and ligand play?

choices.text: Each acts as both acid and base: the ligand donates to the metal, and the metal's d electrons donate into the ligand's π* LUMO
The metal is only a Lewis acid and CO only a Lewis base
choices.why: That describes the M–CO σ bond, but the metal also acts as a base toward the ligand's empty π* orbitals.

choices.text: The metal is only a Lewis base and CO only a Lewis acid
choices.why: The ligand also donates to the metal, forming the σ bond, so each partner plays both roles.

choices.text: Neither, since metal-ligand bonds are ionic
choices.why: The frontier orbital picture describes these bonds as orbital interactions, with the HOMO of each partner interacting with the LUMO of the other.

explanation: Both reactants can act as acid and base, with the HOMO of each interacting with the LUMO of the other. In π-type interactions between a metal with occupied d orbitals and a π-acceptor ligand, the ligand acts as a base and the metal as an acid to give the M–CO single bond, and the metal also acts as a base toward the ligand's π* LUMO orbitals.

prompt: How does the BF3 affinity of a 4-substituted pyridine change when the substituent is changed from electron-donating Me to electron-withdrawing CF3?

choices.text: It decreases slightly, because electron-withdrawing groups make the nitrogen lone pair less available
It increases, because CF3 makes the nitrogen more electron deficient
choices.why: Making a base site more electron deficient lowers its basicity. Electron deficiency increases Lewis acidity, not basicity.

choices.text: It increases sharply, because fluorine is a strong base
choices.why: The fluorines are far from the nitrogen. Their effect is to withdraw electron density, which lowers the nitrogen's basicity.

choices.text: It doesn't change, because the substituent isn't on the nitrogen
choices.why: Inductive effects act through bonds, so substituents on the ring alter the electron density at the nitrogen site.

explanation: Because Lewis acid-base reactions occur at particular sites, substituents that inductively donate or withdraw electron density change those sites' properties. Electron-withdrawing substituents decrease Lewis basicity, and electron-donating ones increase it. The BF3 affinities of 4-substituted pyridines decrease slightly from Me to CF3. The effects are modest and compete with steric, hardness, and π effects.

prompt: Toward most bases, Lewis acidity runs BI3 > BBr3 > BCl3 >> BF3. What explanation does computational work support?

choices.text: The larger halogens are less able to relieve boron's electron deficiency through σ interactions; π donation plays little or no role
π donation from the halogens to boron decreases down the group
choices.why: This is the explanation some textbooks give, but computational work suggests it is incorrect. The differences come mainly from σ overlap.

choices.text: Inductive effects alone: fluorine is most electronegative, so BF3 is the weakest acid
choices.why: Inductive effects alone would predict the opposite: electron-withdrawing F should make BF3 the strongest acid. The observed trend runs counter to inductive effects.

choices.text: Iodine atoms are electron-withdrawing, so BI3 is most electron deficient
choices.why: Iodine is the least electronegative of these halogens. The trend comes from size effects on σ overlap.

explanation: The boron trihalide acidity trend runs counter to inductive effects alone. Some textbooks attribute it to π donation from the halogens decreasing down the group, but computational work suggests that size effects mainly change the extent of σ overlap: the larger halogens are less able to reduce the electron deficiency at boron through σ interactions, and π interactions play little or no role.

prompt: Why are anions such as triflate, PF6^−, and BF4^− useful as weakly coordinating counterions for reactive cations?

choices.text: As conjugate bases of very strong acids, with electron-withdrawing substituents, they are very poor Lewis bases toward metals and other electrophiles
They are strong Lewis bases that bind the cation tightly and protect it
choices.why: A strongly binding anion would react with the cation. These anions are useful because they barely coordinate.

choices.text: They contain no lone pairs at all
choices.why: They do have lone pairs. They are weak Lewis bases because of electron-withdrawing substituents, not because they lack electrons.

choices.text: They are completely inert toward every electrophile
choices.why: All of them react with suitably electrophilic centers, which is why they are better described as weakly coordinating.

explanation: The nonreactivity of superacids' conjugate bases toward H^+ is often mirrored in nonreactivity toward other Lewis acids and electrophiles, notably metals. This makes them useful as noncoordinating ions, though since all react with suitably electrophilic centers they are better understood as weakly coordinating. Triflate, PF6^−, and BF4^− are now commonly used as counterions for isolating reactive cations.

prompt: In a charge transfer (donor-acceptor) complex A^δ−B^δ+, which species is called the donor?

choices.text: The Lewis base, which is a net donor of electron density and negative charge
The Lewis acid, which donates its empty orbital
choices.why: The Lewis acid accepts electron density, so it is the acceptor (A).

choices.text: Whichever species has the larger mass
choices.why: Donor and acceptor are defined by the direction of electron transfer, from base to acid.

choices.text: The species that ends up with a partial negative charge
choices.why: The acceptor gains negative charge (δ−). The donor, the base, ends up partially positive (δ+).

explanation: In weakly bound Lewis acid-base adducts, the transfer of electron density and charge from base to acid is only partial. These are charge transfer (CT) or donor-acceptor (DA) complexes. The base is the donor (D), a net donor of electrons and their negative charge, and the acid is the acceptor (A).

prompt: Iodine is purple in hexane but yellow-brown in donor solvents. What causes the change?

choices.text: I2 forms charge transfer complexes with the donor solvent, and these absorb light in a new charge transfer band
I2 is reduced to I^− by the solvent
choices.why: The color change comes from weak Lewis acid-base association, not full reduction. The complex shows a new charge transfer absorption.

choices.text: Donor solvents break I2 into iodine atoms
choices.why: I2 stays intact. Acting as a Lewis acid, it forms a weak complex with the donor.

choices.text: I2 acts as a Lewis base toward the solvent
choices.why: In iodine charge transfer complexes, I2 is the Lewis acid (acceptor) and the solvent is the donor.

explanation: When iodine is dissolved in donor solvents, the purple color of molecular iodine is replaced by yellow-brown. Charge transfer complexes like those formed by I2 can absorb light in ways neither donor nor acceptor can alone, showing charge transfer bands. In the CT transition, the partial transfer of charge from donor to acceptor is pushed further by photoexcitation: D^δ+−A^δ− → D^+−A^−.

prompt: What happens in a metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) transition?

choices.text: An electron moves from a filled or partly filled metal d orbital to a ligand π*-type orbital
An electron moves from a filled ligand orbital to a metal d orbital
choices.why: That is ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT). MLCT goes from metal to ligand.

choices.text: An electron moves from one d orbital to another on the same metal
choices.why: MLCT moves an electron between the metal and a ligand, not between d orbitals on the metal.

choices.text: An electron moves between two metal centers
choices.why: That is metal-to-metal charge transfer, seen in some bimetallic complexes.

explanation: Charge transfer bands give many transition metal complexes their intense color. MLCT bands involve transfer of an electron from a filled or partly filled metal d orbital to a ligand π*-type orbital. LMCT bands transfer an electron from a ligand orbital to a metal d orbital. The CT excited state is both a better oxidant and a better reductant than the ground state.

prompt: What is the difference between a substance's Lewis basicity and its Lewis base affinity toward a reference acid?

choices.text: Lewis basicity is −ΔG for adduct formation, while Lewis base affinity is −ΔH for the same reaction
Lewis basicity is measured in the gas phase, while affinity is measured in water
choices.why: The distinction is between free energy and enthalpy, not the phase.

choices.text: They are the same quantity under two names
choices.why: They use different thermodynamic quantities: basicity uses ΔG and affinity uses ΔH.

choices.text: Lewis basicity is −ΔH, while affinity is the equilibrium constant
choices.why: Basicity is defined by −ΔG. Affinity uses −ΔH, which is easier to measure.

explanation: Lewis acidities and basicities are defined by the free energy change for adduct formation, B: + A ⇌ B−A, with −ΔG = Lewis basicity of B toward A. Reaction enthalpies are easier to measure, so many scales use −ΔH instead; these enthalpy-based values are called Lewis acid and base affinities.

prompt: Why is there no universal reference scale of Lewis base strength?

choices.text: The strength of a Lewis acid-base interaction depends on the acid's hardness, on steric effects, and on solvent effects
Lewis bases can't be measured experimentally
choices.why: Lewis base affinities are measured, for example on the BF3 and SbCl5 scales. They just depend on the reference acid and conditions.

choices.text: All Lewis bases have the same strength toward every acid
choices.why: Base strength changes markedly with the acid's hardness, so a ranking against one acid may not hold for another.

choices.text: Only Brønsted bases can be ranked on a scale
choices.why: Several Lewis scales exist. None is universal, because hardness, sterics, and solvent change the interaction energy.

explanation: A given base's affinity is not a static parameter. It differs markedly with the acid's hardness (Lewis acids associate more strongly with bases of similar charge density and polarizability), sterically hindered interactions are weaker, and solvents stabilize adduct and free species differently. Predictions from a scale whose reference acid differs much in hardness should be taken as tentative.

prompt: In the BF3 affinity scale of Lewis basicity, what is measured, and why has it largely replaced the Gutmann donor number scale?

choices.text: −ΔH for Base(solution) + BF3(g) → Base−BF3(solution); BF3 adduct energies are easier to correlate with computations than SbCl5 adducts
−ΔH for Base + SbCl5 in 1,2-dichloroethane; SbCl5 is easier to model computationally
choices.why: That reaction defines the Gutmann donor number. The BF3 scale replaced it because BF3 adducts are easier to calculate than SbCl5 adducts.

choices.text: The equilibrium constant for Base + BF3 in water; aqueous data are more reliable
choices.why: The BF3 affinity is an enthalpy, measured for a solution-phase adduct formed with gaseous BF3.

choices.text: ΔG for Base + H^+ in the gas phase; proton affinities are easier to measure
choices.why: That describes gas-phase basicity toward H^+. The BF3 scale uses BF3 as the reference acid.

explanation: Two common scales of Lewis base affinity use SbCl5 and BF3 as reference acids. The Gutmann donor number is −ΔH for forming the base's SbCl5 adduct in dilute 1,2-dichloroethane. The BF3 affinity, −ΔH for Base(solution) + BF3(g) → Base−BF3(solution), has largely supplanted it because energies of BF3 adducts are easier to calculate than those of SbCl5.

prompt: In an organohalogen R–X, where is the σ-hole that lets X act as a Lewis acid in a halogen bond?

choices.text: On X, directly opposite the R–X bond, where electron density is diminished
On X, perpendicular to the R–X bond
choices.why: Perpendicular to the bond, the halogen is Lewis basic. The electrophilic σ-hole is on the far side of X, opposite the R–X bond.

choices.text: On the R group, next to the R–X bond
choices.why: The σ-hole is on the halogen itself, on the side opposite its single bond.

choices.text: Spread evenly around X
choices.why: The charge on X is distributed unevenly, which is what makes halogen bonding directional.

explanation: Singly bonded halogens are electrophilic on the side opposite the bond. In CF3I, the I is Lewis basic perpendicular to the C–I bond and Lewis acidic opposite it. That region of diminished electron density is the σ-hole, and Lewis bases form halogen bonds (XB) along that direction.

prompt: In a halogen bond C–I···N between an iodoarene and an amine, which component is called the halogen bond donor?

choices.text: The iodine (the organohalogen), which acts as the Lewis acid
The amine nitrogen, because it donates its lone pair
choices.why: The naming follows the halogen: the halogen is the halogen bond donor and the base is the halogen bond acceptor, even though the base donates the electron pair.

choices.text: The carbon atom bonded to iodine
choices.why: The halogen itself, here iodine, is the halogen bond donor.

choices.text: Both equally, since the bond is symmetric
choices.why: The roles differ: the halogen is the donor (the Lewis acid) and the base is the acceptor.

explanation: A halogen is said to act as a halogen bond donor when it forms a halogen bond with a base along the direction opposite its R–X bond, with the base acting as the halogen bond acceptor. Here iodine is the donor even though, in Lewis terms, it is the electron-pair acceptor.

prompt: When I2 forms a halogen-bonded adduct with a Lewis base, how do the I–I bond and the I2 π* → σ* absorption change?

choices.text: The I–I bond weakens and the π* → σ* band shifts to higher energy (a blueshift), both more so for stronger donors
The I–I bond strengthens and the band shifts to lower energy
choices.why: Electron density donated into the I2 σ* LUMO weakens the I–I bond, and the π* → σ* transition shifts to higher energy.

choices.text: The I–I bond weakens and the band shifts to lower energy (a redshift)
choices.why: The bond does weaken, but the π* → σ* band is blueshifted to higher energy and shorter wavelength.

choices.text: Neither changes, since halogen bonds are too weak to affect I2
choices.why: Both shift measurably, which is why they are used to rank closely related donors.

explanation: Adduct formation transfers electron density from the base HOMO into the acid LUMO, which alters bonding within the acid. For I2 this weakens the I–I bond and blueshifts the π* → σ* transition to higher energy and shorter wavelength. Both effects increase with the HOMO energy of the Lewis base.

prompt: The I–I stretching shift is 44.5 cm^−1 for tetrahydrothiophene and 27.4 cm^−1 for pyridine, but the π* → σ* blueshifts are 3640 and 4560 cm^−1. What does this show about such spectroscopic measures?

choices.text: They correlate poorly across different types of bases, so they are best used to rank closely related donors
Tetrahydrothiophene must be a stronger base by every measure
choices.why: Its blueshift is smaller than pyridine's, so the two measures disagree. That is why they aren't absolute measures of basicity.

choices.text: The data must be wrong, since the two measures always agree
choices.why: The two measures are imperfectly correlated overall. They correlate well only within a given type of base.

choices.text: Spectroscopic shifts give an absolute scale of Lewis basicity
choices.why: Because the measures disagree across base types, they are not useful as an absolute measure of Lewis basicity.

explanation: The extent of I–I weakening (Δν) and the blueshift of I2's π* → σ* band are imperfectly correlated overall but correlate well for Lewis bases of a given type. So these shifts are not useful as an absolute measure of Lewis basicity, but they can rank the halogen bond affinity of a closely related set of donors.

prompt: When a trivalent boron compound forms an adduct with an amine, the boron changes from trigonal to a more crowded tetrahedral geometry. What kind of steric strain arises from this rearrangement?

choices.text: Back strain (B-strain)
Front strain (F-strain)
choices.why: F-strain is when bulky groups keep the acid and base centers from approaching. B-strain comes from clashes as the geometry rearranges on adduct formation.

choices.text: Internal strain (I-strain)
choices.why: I-strain is the strain of deforming bond and torsional angles from stable local geometries, most important for basic centers in rings or clusters.

choices.text: Torsional strain from the B–N bond rotating
choices.why: The steric classes here are F-, B-, and I-strain. Clashes caused by the trigonal-to-tetrahedral change at boron are B-strain.

explanation: Bulky groups weaken Lewis acids and bases by introducing strain into the adduct. F-strain: bulky groups block the acid and base centers from approaching. B-strain: steric clashes that occur as acid and base rearrange on adduct formation, such as boron going from trigonal to tetrahedral. I-strain: the cost of deforming bond and torsional angles, important in rings and clusters.

prompt: A bulky triarylphosphine and a bulky triarylborane are too hindered to form an adduct. What can the mixture do with H2?

choices.text: Cleave it heterolytically, giving a phosphonium cation and a hydroborate anion
Nothing, since the acid and base can't interact
choices.why: Even though they can't form an adduct, the acid and base can act together on a substrate. This is frustrated Lewis pair chemistry.

choices.text: Form a stable B–P adduct that excludes H2
choices.why: Steric bulk prevents the adduct. The unquenched acid and base sites are what make the pair reactive.

choices.text: Reduce H2 to two hydride ions
choices.why: The H2 is split into H^+ (on P) and H^− (on B), not into two hydrides.

explanation: When a Lewis acid and base are sterically hindered from forming an adduct, they can act together to heterolytically cleave bonds: frustrated Lewis pair (FLP) chemistry. Mixtures of hindered triarylphosphines and triarylboranes cleave H2 into phosphonium and hydroborate ions. This activates substrates, and FLP systems have been developed that catalyze hydrogenations.
